title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A sealed flask contains only neon gas and nitrogen gas. How should its contents be classified?
options: A homogeneous mixture of two elements
A heterogeneous mixture of two compounds
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Neon and nitrogen are elements. The gases mix uniformly without becoming chemically bonded to one another.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which observation most strongly supports the conclusion that a sample is a mixture rather than a pure compound?
options: Different batches can contain different proportions of its components.
It contains more than one type of atom.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Mixtures can have variable composition; a particular pure compound has a fixed ratio of its constituent elements.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A sample consists entirely of identical molecules, each containing one sulfur atom and two oxygen atoms. What is the sample?
options: A mixture of sulfur and oxygen
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Every particle has the same fixed combination of different elements, so the sample is a pure compound.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Liquid bromine contains only Br₂ molecules. Which classification is correct?
options: An element, because all atoms have the same atomic number
A mixture, because many molecules are present
A compound, because it is liquid
A compound, because each molecule has two atoms
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: An element can exist as diatomic molecules. The number of atoms per molecule does not determine whether it is a compound.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A beaker contains liquid water with floating ice, and no other substances. How is this sample best described?
options: A mixture of two chemical compounds
A new compound formed from ice and water
A pure substance present in two physical states
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Both phases consist of H₂O. More than one physical state does not by itself make a sample a mixture.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which statement distinguishes a compound from a mixture?
options: A mixture must have components visible to the naked eye.
A mixture must contain at least one liquid.
Separating a compound into its constituent elements requires chemical change.
A compound must contain atoms in a variable ratio.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: A compound contains chemically bonded elements; the components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A clear solution of sodium chloride is sampled from its top and bottom after thorough mixing. What should be expected?
options: The two samples must have different chemical formulas for water.
Both samples have the same composition, provided no evaporation occurs.
The top sample contains only water.
The bottom sample contains only sodium chloride.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: A homogeneous mixture is uniform in composition on the scale of ordinary sampling.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A mixture contains insoluble sand and aqueous sodium chloride. Which sequence can recover dry sand and solid sodium chloride separately?
options: Evaporate all the water, then filter the dry residue
Filter, then evaporate water from the filtrate
Distil the sand before dissolving the salt
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Filtration separates sand from the salt solution. Evaporating the filtrate leaves the dissolved salt.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: During filtration of a suspension, what is the filtrate?
options: Only chemically pure solvent in every case
The liquid, including dissolved substances, that passes through the filter
The filter paper and all material on it
Only the insoluble solid retained on the filter
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Filtration removes particles of insoluble material; dissolved substances generally pass through with the solvent.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Why does filtering a sodium chloride solution through ordinary filter paper fail to produce pure water?
options: Water molecules cannot pass through filter paper.
The filter converts sodium chloride into a gas.
The dissolved ions pass through the filter with the water.
Sodium chloride must first become an element.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Ordinary filtration does not separate a dissolved solute from its solvent.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A student wants to recover pure water from a solution of a non-volatile salt. Which process is appropriate?
options: Evaporation with the vapour allowed to escape
Simple distillation with collection of the condensate
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Water vaporizes and can be condensed separately while the non-volatile salt remains in the flask.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A solid is very soluble in hot water but only slightly soluble in cold water. Which method is suitable for obtaining purified crystals from a crude sample, assuming the impurities remain dissolved on cooling?
options: Mixing the solid with more insoluble impurities
Filtering a cold solution without cooling it further
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Dissolving in hot solvent and cooling allows the desired solid to crystallize while the specified impurities remain in solution.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Two miscible liquids have boiling points of 65 °C and 82 °C. What normally becomes enriched in the first fraction collected during fractional distillation?
options: A new compound with boiling point 147 °C
The liquid with the lower boiling point
The liquid with the higher boiling point
Both liquids in exactly their initial proportions at all times
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The more volatile component contributes a larger proportion of the vapour and is enriched in the early distillate.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Dry ice changes directly from solid carbon dioxide into gas. What is this change called?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Water droplets form on the outside of a cold glass when water vapour in the surrounding air changes state. Which change occurs?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Water changes from gas to liquid, which is condensation.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which description applies to the particles in a liquid?
options: They remain close together but can move past one another.
They have no attractive interactions with neighbouring particles.
They occupy widely separated fixed positions.
They remain at rest unless the liquid boils.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Liquid particles are close together and mobile, allowing a liquid to flow while retaining a nearly fixed volume.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A pure solid is heated at constant pressure and melts at its melting point. Why can its temperature remain constant while energy is supplied?
options: The solid must lose all of its mass.
Energy changes particle interactions rather than increasing average kinetic energy during melting.
All particles stop moving during melting.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: During a phase change at constant temperature, the energy supplied does not increase the particles' average kinetic energy.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A laboratory is at 27 °C. What is its temperature in kelvin, to the nearest kelvin?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: T/K = temperature/°C + 273.15, so 27 °C is 300.15 K, approximately 300 K.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A sample warms from 15 °C to 33 °C. What is its temperature increase in kelvin?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Kelvin and Celsius intervals have the same size: 33 − 15 = 18 °C corresponds to 18 K.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A gas is heated from 250 K to 500 K. What happens to the average kinetic energy of its particles?
options: It increases by a factor of four.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature; 500/250 = 2.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A neutral atom has atomic number 17 and mass number 37. How many neutrons does it contain?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The neutron number is mass number minus atomic number: 37 − 17 = 20.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: An ion has 13 protons, 14 neutrons and 10 electrons. What is its charge?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The charge is the number of protons minus the number of electrons: 13 − 10 = +3.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: How many electrons are present in an oxide ion, O²⁻, if oxygen has atomic number 8?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The ion has two more electrons than the neutral atom: 8 + 2 = 10.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which pair represents isotopes of the same element?
options: Atoms with 6 and 8 protons, each having a neutral charge
Atoms with respectively 6 and 8 protons, each with 6 neutrons
Atoms with 6 protons and respectively 6 and 8 neutrons
Atoms with respectively 6 and 7 protons, each with mass number 14
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Isotopes have the same proton number and different neutron numbers.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which change would convert an atom of one element into an atom of a different element?
options: Changing only the number of neutrons
Changing the number of protons in the nucleus
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The proton number defines the element; changes in electrons form ions and changes in neutrons form isotopes.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: An atom of calcium-44 has atomic number 20. What remains unchanged when it forms Ca²⁺?
options: Its numbers of protons and neutrons
Its number of electrons and its charge
Its charge and its proton number
Its electron number and neutron number
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Ion formation changes the number of electrons, not the composition of the nucleus.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which statement correctly compares a proton with an electron?
options: They have identical charges and identical masses.
They have opposite charges and approximately equal masses.
They have opposite charges of equal magnitude, but the proton has a much greater mass.
The electron has a positive charge and the proton a negative charge.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: A proton has relative charge +1 and an electron −1; the electron's mass is very small relative to the proton's.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Why is most of an atom's mass concentrated in its nucleus?
options: The nucleus contains all the atom's electrons.
The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, which are much more massive than electrons.
The nucleus occupies most of the atom's volume.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Protons and neutrons account for almost all atomic mass, although the nucleus occupies a very small volume.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A neutral atom contains 35 electrons and 45 neutrons. What is its mass number?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: A neutral atom has 35 protons, so its mass number is 35 + 45 = 80.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: An ion with charge 2− contains 18 electrons and 18 neutrons. What is its atomic number?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: A 2− ion has two more electrons than protons, so the proton number is 18 − 2 = 16.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A hypothetical element has isotopes of mass numbers 10 and 11, with abundances of 20% and 80%. Using the mass numbers as isotopic masses, what is its relative atomic mass?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The weighted mean is (10 × 20 + 11 × 80)/100 = 10.8.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: An element has only two isotopes, with masses taken as 63 and 65. Its relative atomic mass is 63.4. What is the percentage abundance of the isotope of mass 65?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: If x is the fraction of the heavier isotope, 63(1 − x) + 65x = 63.4; x = 0.20.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: An element has isotopes of mass numbers 24, 25 and 26 with abundances of 50%, 20% and 30%. Taking these mass numbers as isotopic masses, what is its relative atomic mass?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Two samples of the same element have different relative atomic masses. Which explanation can account for this?
options: Relative atomic mass changes whenever a sample changes state.
Every atom in one sample has a different proton number from every atom in the other.
All neutrons have been converted into electrons in one sample.
The samples contain different proportions of the element's isotopes.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Changing isotopic abundances changes the weighted mean atomic mass without changing the identity of the element.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which statement about neutral atoms of carbon-12 and carbon-14 is correct?
options: They have the same number of electrons and different numbers of neutrons.
Carbon-14 has two more protons than carbon-12.
They have different electron configurations because their mass numbers differ.
They have different numbers of protons and the same number of neutrons.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Both isotopes have six protons and six electrons; they have six and eight neutrons respectively.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A species has 9 protons, 10 neutrons and 10 electrons. Which description is correct?
options: A fluoride ion with mass number 19 and charge 1−
A neon atom with mass number 20
A fluorine atom with mass number 19 and no charge
A fluoride ion with mass number 10 and charge 1+
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Nine protons identify fluorine, 9 + 10 = 19 gives the mass number, and the extra electron gives charge −1.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Atoms X and Y both have mass number 40. X has 18 protons and Y has 20 protons. Which statement is correct?
options: X and Y must be isotopes of the same element.
X and Y are different elements, and X has two more neutrons than Y.
X has two fewer neutrons than Y.
X and Y have the same number of neutrons.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Their neutron numbers are 22 and 20. Equal mass numbers do not imply the same element.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which species has the same number of electrons as a neutral neon atom (atomic number 10)?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Mg²⁺ has 12 − 2 = 10 electrons. The other species have 11, 9 and 12 respectively.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: An element has two naturally occurring isotopes with masses taken as 79 and 81. The isotope of mass 81 becomes more abundant in a sample. What happens to the sample's relative atomic mass?
options: It remains exactly 80 regardless of abundance.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Increasing the weight of the heavier isotope increases the mean, which remains between the two isotope masses.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: In a nuclear symbol, which quantity is given by the upper-left number, A?
options: The number of neutrons minus the number of protons
The total number of protons and electrons
The total number of protons and neutrons
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: A is the mass number, also called the nucleon number; it excludes electrons.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Phosphorus has atomic number 15. Which is its ground-state electron configuration?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Fifteen electrons fill the lower-energy sublevels before giving 3s²3p³ in the outer main energy level.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which is the electron configuration of Cl⁻, given that chlorine has atomic number 17?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The chloride ion has 18 electrons, one more than the neutral chlorine atom.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Cobalt has atomic number 27 and the neutral configuration [Ar]3d⁷4s². Which is the configuration of Co²⁺?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The two 4s electrons are removed when Co²⁺ forms.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of copper, atomic number 29?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Copper is an exception to the simplest filling pattern and has a filled 3d sublevel with one 4s electron.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A neutral atom has configuration [Ne]3s²3p¹. What is its atomic number?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The neon core accounts for 10 electrons, and 3s²3p¹ adds three more. A neutral atom therefore has 13 protons.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: What is the maximum number of electrons in the third main energy level?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: A main energy level can hold 2n² electrons; with n = 3, this is 18.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: How many orbitals are present in a p sublevel?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: A p sublevel contains three orbitals with different spatial orientations; each can hold two electrons.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: What is the maximum number of electrons that a d sublevel can contain?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: A d sublevel contains five orbitals, each capable of holding two electrons.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a p orbital from a p sublevel?
options: A p sublevel contains only one orbital.
One p orbital holds at most two electrons, while a complete p sublevel holds at most six.
One p orbital holds six electrons, while a p sublevel holds two.
A p orbital consists of three main energy levels.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The p sublevel contains three p orbitals, each with a two-electron capacity.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Two electrons occupy the same orbital. Which arrangement is allowed?
options: One must have a positive charge.
They must belong to different main energy levels.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The Pauli exclusion principle requires the two electrons in one orbital to have opposite spins.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Three electrons occupy the three p orbitals of an isolated atom in its ground state. Which arrangement follows Hund's rule?
options: One electron in each orbital, with all three having different charges
One electron in each orbital, with parallel spins
Two electrons in one orbital and one in another, leaving the third empty
All three electrons in one orbital
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Degenerate orbitals are occupied singly with parallel spins before electrons pair.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: How many unpaired electrons are present in the 2p sublevel of a ground-state oxygen atom with configuration 1s²2s²2p⁴?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: For p⁴, three orbitals first receive one electron each; the fourth pairs in one, leaving two unpaired electrons.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which feature correctly describes an s atomic orbital?
options: It consists of two directional lobes separated by the nucleus.
It is a fixed circular path followed by an electron.
It can hold six electrons with the same spin.
Its probability distribution is spherically symmetric about the nucleus.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: An s orbital is spherically symmetric. An orbital describes an electron probability distribution, not a fixed path.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: What happens when an electron in an isolated hydrogen atom moves from n = 2 to n = 5?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Moving to a higher energy level requires absorption of energy.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which electron transition in hydrogen emits ultraviolet radiation by ending at the first main energy level?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Emission to n = 1 belongs to the ultraviolet region; the upward transition is absorption.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which transition in hydrogen can produce a visible emission line?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Visible hydrogen emission lines arise from higher levels falling to n = 2.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Blue light and red light travel at the same speed in a vacuum. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both have the same frequency because their speeds are equal.
Blue light has a lower frequency and lower photon energy than red light.
Blue light has a longer wavelength and higher frequency than red light.
Blue light has a higher frequency and higher photon energy than red light.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Blue light has a shorter wavelength, hence a higher frequency and higher photon energy.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Why does a hydrogen discharge tube produce separate emission lines instead of every possible colour?
options: Only certain differences between electron energy levels are possible.
Every photon emitted by hydrogen must have the same energy.
Electrons can have any energy but emit only by chance.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Discrete allowed electron energies produce photons with specific energies when transitions occur.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: As the main energy level n increases in hydrogen, how does the spacing between adjacent energy levels change?
options: The levels become farther apart by a constant amount.
Every higher level has less energy than n = 1.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Hydrogen energy levels converge at higher energies, so adjacent levels become closer together.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: An electron falls between two energy levels separated by a larger energy gap than in another transition. How does the emitted photon compare?
options: It has higher frequency and shorter wavelength.
It has lower energy and shorter wavelength.
It has lower frequency and longer wavelength.
It has the same frequency but greater speed in a vacuum.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: A larger energy gap gives a higher-energy photon; frequency increases while wavelength decreases.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which formula results when Li⁺ and O²⁻ form an electrically neutral ionic compound?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Two Li⁺ ions are required to balance the charge of one O²⁻ ion.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: What is the formula of the ionic compound formed from Al³⁺ and O²⁻?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Two aluminium ions provide +6 and three oxide ions provide −6.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: What is the formula of magnesium hydroxide?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Mg²⁺ requires two hydroxide ions, each with charge −1.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which is the formula of calcium nitrate?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Calcium is Ca²⁺ and nitrate is NO₃⁻, so two nitrate ions are needed.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: What is the formula of ammonium sulfate?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Two NH₄⁺ ions balance one SO₄²⁻ ion.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which name correctly describes Cu₂O?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The oxide ion has charge −2, so each of the two copper ions must have charge +1.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: What is the formula of iron(III) chloride?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Iron(III) is Fe³⁺; three chloride ions are needed per iron ion.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which is the correct name for NaHCO₃?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The anion HCO₃⁻ is hydrogencarbonate; carbonate is CO₃²⁻.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A main-group atom has outer-shell configuration 3s²3p⁵. Which ion does it normally form to achieve a noble-gas configuration?
options: A 1+ ion by losing one electron
A 2− ion by gaining two neutrons
A 5+ ion by losing five protons
A 1− ion by gaining one electron
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Seven outer-shell electrons become eight when one electron is gained, giving charge −1.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Why does losing two electrons from a neutral magnesium atom produce a positive ion?
options: The two lost electrons had positive charge.
The ion has gained two protons.
The ion has two more protons than electrons.
The ion has lost two neutrons.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The nucleus is unchanged; removing negatively charged electrons leaves a net positive charge.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which statement describes the ionic bond in sodium fluoride?
options: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
Attraction between positive ions and a sea of delocalized electrons
Sharing of a single pair of electrons between two neutral atoms
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between cations and anions.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity while solid sodium chloride does not conduct appreciably?
options: It contains ions only after melting.
The solid has no charged particles.
Its ions can move through the liquid but are fixed in the solid lattice.
Melting converts all chloride ions into free electrons.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Mobile ions transport charge in the melt; the solid contains ions but they cannot move through the lattice.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: A substance has a high melting point, does not conduct electricity as a solid, and conducts when molten. Which structure best explains these observations?
options: Separate atoms of a noble gas
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: The observations are characteristic of an ionic solid whose ions become mobile on melting.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: What does the formula CaF₂ represent in a crystal of calcium fluoride?
options: Individual CaF₂ molecules held together by hydrogen bonds
A 2:1 ratio of calcium ions to fluoride ions
A 1:2 ratio of calcium ions to fluoride ions in an extended lattice
Two calcium atoms sharing one electron with one fluorine atom
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: An ionic formula expresses the simplest electrically neutral ratio of ions, not discrete molecules.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Two ionic solids have ions of the same charge but different ionic radii. Which change generally strengthens the electrostatic attraction?
options: Removing all charges from the ions
Increasing the distance between the ion centres
Decreasing the distance between the ion centres
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: For fixed charges, electrostatic attraction increases as the separation decreases.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Two hypothetical ionic lattices have similar distances between neighbouring ions. Lattice X contains 1+ and 1− ions; lattice Y contains 2+ and 2− ions. Which has stronger attraction between neighbouring unlike ions?
options: X, because its ions have smaller charge magnitudes
Y, because the magnitudes of the ionic charges are larger
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: At similar separations, larger ionic charge magnitudes give stronger electrostatic attraction.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Why do many ionic compounds have low volatility?
options: They consist of weakly attracted gas molecules.
Their ions become uncharged whenever heated.
Substantial energy is needed to overcome strong attractions throughout the lattice.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Strong lattice attractions make it difficult for particles to escape into the gas phase.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which statement about ionic compounds is correct?
options: Every ionic compound consists of discrete two-ion molecules.
Their solubility in water varies; not all ionic compounds dissolve readily.
Every ionic compound is highly soluble in water.
All ionic compounds conduct electricity well as solids.
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: An ionic structure does not guarantee high water solubility; properties depend on the particular compound.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: Which substance contains covalent bonds within a polyatomic ion and ionic attractions between ions?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Ammonium chloride has covalent N–H bonds within NH₄⁺ and ionic attractions between NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: An ionic compound contains M³⁺ and sulfate ions, SO₄²⁻. What is its empirical formula?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Two M³⁺ ions and three sulfate ions give charges of +6 and −6.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: What holds the two hydrogen atoms together in an H₂ molecule?
options: Attraction between two negative hydrogen ions
Repulsion between the two positive nuclei
Hydrogen bonding between the two atoms
Attraction between the shared electron pair and both positive nuclei
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: A covalent bond involves a shared electron pair attracted to the positively charged nuclei of both atoms.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: How many electrons are shared in the N≡N bond of nitrogen gas?
hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: A triple bond contains three shared electron pairs, hence six bonding electrons.

title: Multiple-choice practice
prompt: For bonds between the same pair of elements, how does a triple bond generally compare with a single bond?
options: It has the same length and strength.

hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
working: Both bonding electrons initially come from the donor; after formation it is a covalent bond. The result is 2.

hint: Identify the relevant relationship or definition, work out your answer, then compare the four options.
